analysis.one_liner: Requires corporations receiving federal COVID-19 aid to pay $15 an hour, give paid leave, and cap CEO pay.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Any corporation that received federal COVID-19 rescue money — emergency Fed lending, grants, loans, or loan guarantees — would have to give every worker at least 14 days of fully paid leave, pay everyone at least $15 an hour (including part-time and tipped workers), and keep the CEO's pay within 50 times the pay of the typical worker. The Securities and Exchange Commission would enforce the rules. The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at corporations receiving federal COVID-19 aid: they would get at least 14 days of fully paid leave and a $15 minimum wage, including part-time and tipped workers. Taxpayers also benefit indirectly, since their rescue money would carry conditions instead of flowing out with no strings attached.

how_it_helps.text: Requires at least 14 days of fully paid leave for all workers at corporations receiving federal COVID-19 aid, during the covered period.

Requires a $15-an-hour minimum wage for every employee of those corporations, including full-time, part-time, and tipped workers, beginning no later than January 1, 2021, and expresses the sense of Congress that contractors should pay the same wage.
Bars a CEO-to-median-worker pay ratio above 50 to 1 at those corporations and prohibits any officer or employee from earning more than the CEO.

Covers any federal COVID-19 aid: emergency lending under section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act and any federal grant, loan, or loan guarantee, with requirements lasting until one year after the emergency ends or the aid is repaid.
Gives the Securities and Exchange Commission authority to enforce the requirements and write the necessary rules.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations receiving federal COVID-19 aid would bear the cost: higher wage bills (especially for part-time and tipped workers), the cost of paid leave, and reduced top executive compensation. Companies with pay ratios far above 50 to 1 would face the largest adjustments.
analysis.who_pays_short: Companies taking federal COVID-19 rescue money

drawbacks.text: The wage and leave mandates apply only to companies that took federal aid, creating two tiers of workers doing similar jobs at neighboring firms — one covered by a $15 floor, one not.
The 50-to-1 pay ratio cap and the ban on anyone out-earning the CEO are blunt instruments that could push compensation into harder-to-trace forms rather than actually reducing it.

Requirements would last a covered period of at least a year past the emergency's end or repayment, and companies could argue the mandates punish firms for accepting rescue money, potentially deterring some from participating in support programs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete and well targeted at a moment when federal money was flowing to large companies with few conditions: a $15 wage floor for part-time and tipped workers and guaranteed paid leave during a pandemic. The costs fall on the specific firms that chose to take public money, which is the point of the bill. The pay-ratio cap is the weakest part, since it is easy to structure around, but the wage and leave provisions are straightforward and enforceable.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced the bill on May 12, 2020, with Representative Maxine Waters joining as an original cosponsor.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor beyond the sponsor in a 435-member House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations that received federal COVID-19 aid came out ahead: they kept federal rescue money with no added wage, leave, or executive-pay conditions. The two million or more companies in loan and aid programs continued operating under whatever terms the original CARES Act set.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Corporations that took federal COVID aid

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — the only cosponsor recorded besides the sponsor's original partner.

against.name: House Committee on Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 12, 2020 and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill sat there until the Congress ended.

against.name: House leadership

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes on the bill, so no party split is recorded; both named supporters were Democrats and no Republican supported it, but the bill died in committee before any partisan test.

industries.note: These firms would have had to pay a $15 minimum wage, give 14 days of paid leave, and cap executive pay relative to the median worker as a condition of public rescue money. The bill's central fight was whether public money should come with worker protections; without it, the aid carried no such strings.

industries.industry: Federal Reserve emergency-lending programs and their large borrowers
industries.note: Section 13(3) emergency lending had already flowed to large corporations under the CARES Act without wage or pay-ratio conditions. The bill would have retroactively attached conditions; its death left those programs' original unconditioned structure in place.
The SEC would have gained new enforcement authority over aid recipients' wages, leave, and executive pay, expanding its role from disclosure regulator to enforcer of labor and pay standards.
